metadata.title: Assisted Vaginal Birth
metadata.organization: Royal College of Obstetricians and Gynaecologists
metadata.summary: This guideline addresses rotational and non-rotational assisted vaginal birth using forceps or vacuum extraction. It covers preparation, indications, safety criteria, consent, choice of instrument, conduct and discontinuation of procedures, and postnatal care. It also addresses training, documentation, adverse-event management and priorities for further research.

target_population: Women for whom assisted vaginal birth is being considered or has been attempted
Babies born following attempted assisted vaginal birth

conditions.name: Assisted vaginal birth
conditions.description: Birth assisted with vacuum extraction or forceps for maternal or fetal indications. Decisions about intervention depend on clinical findings, the woman's preferences and the operator's experience; no indication is absolute.
conditions.epidemiology: In the UK, between 10% and 15% of women have an assisted vaginal birth. Almost one in every three nulliparous women gives birth with vacuum extraction or forceps, with lower rates in midwifery-led settings.
conditions.clinical_presentation: Potential indications include suspected fetal compromise, lack of continuing progress in the second stage, maternal exhaustion or distress, and a medical need to avoid the Valsalva manoeuvre. Maternal and fetal indications may occur together.

subtypes.name: Outlet
subtypes.distinguishing_features: The fetal scalp is visible without separating the labia, the skull has reached the perineum, and rotation does not exceed 45°.

subtypes.name: Low
subtypes.distinguishing_features: The fetal skull is at station + 2 cm but has not reached the perineum; the subdivisions are non-rotational ≤ 45° and rotational > 45°.

subtypes.name: Mid
subtypes.distinguishing_features: No more than one-fifth of the fetal head is palpable abdominally, and the leading point of the skull is at station 0 or + 1 cm; the subdivisions are non-rotational ≤ 45° and rotational > 45°.

diagnostic_workup.purpose: Assess how much of the fetal head is palpable and contribute to classification of the proposed birth.
diagnostic_workup.interpretation: The head should be ≤ 1/5 palpable abdominally and is not palpable in most cases. With a deflexed occipito posterior position, up to one-fifth may remain palpable when the skull is at station 0 cm or below.

diagnostic_workup.purpose: Establish cervical dilatation, membrane status, fetal head station and position, caput, moulding and pelvic adequacy.
diagnostic_workup.interpretation: The cervix should be fully dilated, membranes ruptured and the head at the ischial spines or lower. Caput and moulding should be no more than moderate (or +2). Overlapping parietal bones that cannot be reduced constitute severe moulding or +3 and indicate cephalopelvic disproportion.

diagnostic_workup.test: Abdominal ultrasound assessment of fetal head position
diagnostic_workup.purpose: Clarify fetal head position more reliably than clinical examination.
diagnostic_workup.when_indicated: Before assisted vaginal birth when clinical examination leaves the position uncertain.

diagnostic_workup.test: Abdominal or perineal ultrasound assessment of fetal head station, flexion and descent
diagnostic_workup.purpose: Assess station, flexion or direction of descent in the second stage of labour.
diagnostic_workup.interpretation: The guideline finds insufficient evidence and standardisation to support routine use for these assessments.

diagnostic_workup.when_indicated: When assessing a fetal indication for intervention.
diagnostic_workup.interpretation: A pathological result is listed among findings indicating suspected fetal compromise.

diagnostic_workup.when_indicated: When assessing a fetal indication for intervention.
diagnostic_workup.interpretation: An abnormal result is listed among findings indicating suspected fetal compromise.

diagnostic_workup.purpose: Record neonatal findings after an attempted assisted vaginal birth.
diagnostic_workup.when_indicated: Following every attempt at assisted vaginal birth.

diagnostic_workup.test: Measurement of first void and post void residual
diagnostic_workup.when_indicated: Record the timing and volume of the first void after birth; measure the post void residual if retention is suspected.

definitions.description: The fetal scalp can be seen without separating the labia, the skull is at the perineum, and rotation is no greater than 45°.
The fetal skull is at station + 2 cm without being on the perineum. Its subdivisions are non-rotational ≤ 45° and rotational > 45°.
At most one-fifth of the fetal head is palpable abdominally and the leading skull point is at station 0 or + 1 cm. Its subdivisions are non-rotational ≤ 45° and rotational > 45°.

staging.additional_rules: Classification requires abdominal and vaginal examination. Marked caput can make the vertex appear lower than its actual position.

follow_up.schedule: Assess the woman before hospital discharge to explain the indication, address complications and discuss future births. Persistent PTSD symptoms at 1 month warrant referral to skilled professionals. Physiotherapy-directed strategies are offered to reduce urinary incontinence at 3 months.
recommended_tests: Monitor and document the timing and volume of the first postpartum void.
Measure post void residual urine when retention is suspected.
Reassess venous thromboembolism risk after birth.
Assess the neonate for traumatic injury after a failed attempt or sequential instrument use; signs may not be apparent immediately.
long_term_effects: Pelvic floor symptoms discussed in the guideline include pain, dyspareunia, and urinary and bowel incontinence.
Postpartum urinary retention can be associated with long-term bladder dysfunction.
Psychological morbidity and PTSD symptoms may follow childbirth.
follow_up.survivorship_notes: Counsel women about the high likelihood of spontaneous vaginal birth in a subsequent pregnancy. Individualise future-birth planning after a third- or fourth-degree perineal tear or with continuing pelvic floor morbidity.

conditions.name: vacuum-assisted birth
conditions.description: A form of assisted vaginal birth using a vacuum extractor. Compared with forceps, completion with a single instrument is more likely to fail, while maternal perineal trauma is less likely. Soft cups have more failures but less neonatal scalp trauma than rigid cups.

subtypes.name: rotational vacuum extraction
subtypes.distinguishing_features: A vacuum option for rotational birth that requires an experienced operator.

diagnostic_workup.test: Assessment of instrument placement, fetal head position and descent
diagnostic_workup.purpose: Determine whether the extraction is progressing and whether technique, position diagnosis or cephalopelvic disproportion needs reassessment.
diagnostic_workup.when_indicated: Before and during vacuum-assisted birth, particularly if the first two pulls produce minimal descent.
diagnostic_workup.interpretation: Absent progressive descent with moderate traction using a correctly applied instrument is a reason to discontinue the attempt. Two ‘pop-offs’ are also a stopping criterion.

recommended_tests: After a failed vacuum attempt, particularly with multiple pulls, ‘pop-offs’ or sequential instruments, monitor the neonate for injury that may not be immediately evident.
follow_up.survivorship_notes: Following failed vacuum-assisted birth or sequential instrument use, inform the neonatologist so that the baby receives appropriate care.

conditions.name: forceps birth
conditions.description: A form of assisted vaginal birth using forceps. Compared with vacuum extraction, birth is more likely to be completed with a single instrument, but maternal perineal trauma is more likely.

subtypes.name: Kielland’s rotational forceps
subtypes.distinguishing_features: An option for rotational birth that requires specific expertise and training.

diagnostic_workup.test: Assessment of forceps application, handle approximation and progressive fetal descent
diagnostic_workup.purpose: Evaluate correct application and progress during an attempted forceps birth.
diagnostic_workup.when_indicated: During forceps birth, particularly when descent is minimal with the first one or two pulls.
diagnostic_workup.interpretation: Difficulty applying the forceps or approximating their handles, or absent progressive descent with moderate traction, calls for discontinuation. If birth is not imminent after three pulls with a correctly applied instrument used by an experienced operator, the attempt should stop.

recommended_tests: After a failed forceps attempt, particularly with multiple pulls or more than one instrument, monitor the neonate for traumatic injury that may not be apparent at birth.
follow_up.survivorship_notes: Inform the neonatologist after a failed attempt so that the baby receives appropriate care. If caesarean birth follows failed forceps, anticipate possible fetal head impaction.

conditions.name: rotational assisted vaginal birth
conditions.description: An assisted vaginal birth requiring rotation of the fetal head. It demands experienced operators and has higher maternal and neonatal morbidity than less complex assisted births, regardless of instrument.

subtypes.name: Kielland’s rotational forceps
subtypes.distinguishing_features: Rotational forceps technique requiring specific training and expertise.

subtypes.name: manual rotation followed by direct traction forceps or vacuum
subtypes.distinguishing_features: The fetal head is rotated manually before extraction with the selected instrument.

subtypes.name: rotational vacuum extraction
subtypes.distinguishing_features: Rotation is undertaken during vacuum extraction.

diagnostic_workup.purpose: Establish fetal head position, station, degree of rotation and suitability for the proposed birth.
diagnostic_workup.when_indicated: Before attempting rotational assisted vaginal birth.
diagnostic_workup.interpretation: Rotational subdivisions in the classification involve rotation > 45°. Midpelvic birth has a leading skull point at station 0 or + 1 cm and no more than one-fifth of the head palpable abdominally.

diagnostic_workup.test: Ultrasound assessment of fetal head position
diagnostic_workup.purpose: Resolve uncertainty about position after clinical examination.
diagnostic_workup.when_indicated: Before assisted vaginal birth when fetal head position remains uncertain.

definitions.description: The fetal skull is at station + 2 cm but not on the perineum; its rotational subdivision requires rotation > 45°.
No more than one-fifth of the head is palpable abdominally, the leading skull point is at station 0 or + 1 cm, and the rotational subdivision requires rotation > 45°.

staging.additional_rules: A rotational or midpelvic attempt requires supervision from the outset by an experienced operator competent in midpelvic births.

recommended_tests: Following an unsuccessful attempt, assess the neonate for traumatic injury that may not be evident immediately.
follow_up.survivorship_notes: When counselling after a complex assisted vaginal birth in theatre, the guideline describes an approximately 80% likelihood of spontaneous vaginal birth in a subsequent pregnancy.

toxicities.incidence: For births between 32+0 and 36+6 weeks of gestation, a retrospective population-based study reported 0.16% with vacuum extraction versus 0% with forceps birth. The guideline's risk information describes 3 to 6 in 1000, predominantly with vacuum.
recognition: Neonatal traumatic injury may not be apparent immediately after birth.

management.severity: Following failed vacuum-assisted birth, particularly with multiple pulls, ‘pop-offs’ or more than one instrument
management.actions: Inform the neonatologist and monitor the baby for traumatic injury.

prevention: Avoid vacuum birth below 32 weeks of gestation and exercise caution between 32+0 and 36+0 weeks of gestation.
Avoid sequential instrument use whenever possible.

toxicities.event: Intracranial haemorrhage and other serious neonatal traumatic injury
toxicities.incidence: The guideline's risk information gives intracranial haemorrhage with vacuum and forceps as 5 to 15 in 10 000. In a review of 583 340 liveborn singleton infants of nulliparous women, subdural or cerebral haemorrhage occurred in 1 in 860 vacuum births, 1 in 664 forceps births and 1 in 954 caesarean births during labour; with sequential vacuum and forceps use, the rate was 1 in 256. For births between 32+0 and 36+6 weeks of gestation, a retrospective population-based study reported intracranial haemorrhage in 0.12% with vacuum extraction versus 0% with forceps birth.
recognition: Traumatic injury may not be evident immediately after birth.
The guideline includes subgaleal haemorrhage, brachial plexus injury, fracture, facial nerve palsy and cerebral haemorrhage in its neonatal trauma composite.

management.severity: Failed vacuum-assisted or forceps birth, or sequential instrument use
management.actions: Notify the neonatologist and ensure that the baby is assessed and monitored for potentially delayed signs of traumatic injury.

prevention: Avoid sequential instruments whenever possible; an inexperienced operator should not use them without direct supervision.
Avoid vacuum extraction below 32 weeks of gestation and use it cautiously between 32+0 and 36+0 weeks of gestation.
Discontinue an assisted birth when the specified criteria for lack of progress or instrument difficulty are met.

toxicities.event: Neonatal scalp trauma, lacerations and cephalhaematoma
toxicities.incidence: For births between 32+0 and 36+6 weeks of gestation, a retrospective population-based study reported scalp trauma in 9.8% with vacuum extraction versus 6.3% with forceps birth. The guideline's risk information gives facial or scalp lacerations with vacuum and forceps as 10%, and cephalhaematoma, predominantly with vacuum, as 1–12%. A review comparing vacuum with forceps reported greater likelihood of cephalhaematoma with vacuum (OR 2.4; 95% CI 1.7–3.4).
prevention: Use vacuum cautiously at preterm gestational ages as specified in the guideline.
Select the instrument according to the clinical situation and operator expertise; soft vacuum cups have less neonatal scalp trauma but fail more often.

toxicities.event: Obstetric anal sphincter injury (OASI) and other maternal perineal trauma
toxicities.incidence: The guideline's risk information gives OASI as 1–4% with vacuum and 8–12% with forceps; significant vulvo–vaginal tears as 10% with vacuum and 20% with forceps. In a UK cohort of 1360 nulliparous women, OASI occurred in 17.4% with sequential instruments versus 8.4% with forceps alone (OR 2.1, 95% CI 1.2–33).

management.severity: Third- or fourth-degree tear or continuing pelvic floor morbidity
management.actions: Individualise subsequent care and discuss the risk of recurrence and implications for future births.

prevention: Discuss mediolateral episiotomy before assisted vaginal birth. Decide whether to perform it according to the circumstances and the woman's preferences; evidence for OASI prevention is stronger in nulliparous women and forceps births.
When performing mediolateral episiotomy, initiate the cut as the head distends the perineum, at a 60 degree angle.
Avoid sequential instrument use whenever possible.

toxicities.incidence: The guideline's risk information gives postpartum haemorrhage with vacuum and forceps as 10–40%. In a UK prospective study of assisted vaginal births, episiotomy was associated with postpartum haemorrhage in 28.4% versus 18.4% without episiotomy (OR 1.72, 95% CI 1.21–2.45).

management.actions: Submit an incident report as part of risk management.

prevention: Anticipate postpartum haemorrhage when preparing personnel and facilities for assisted vaginal birth.

toxicities.incidence: A small ‘before and after’ trial reported covert PUR in 15/23 (65%) in the observational group versus 2/11 (18%) following systematic intermittent bladder catheterisation at 2 hours post birth (P = 0.02); the guideline notes that the study was small and subject to bias.
recognition: Monitor and record the time and volume of the first void.
Measure post void residual urine if retention is suspected; bladder scanning can be used by appropriately trained personnel.

management.severity: After a trial of assisted vaginal birth with regional analgesia
management.actions: Offer an indwelling catheter for 6–12 hours after birth, in line with local protocol, followed by fluid balance charts to check voiding volumes.

prevention: Explain the risk of retention and the importance of emptying the bladder postpartum.
After regional analgesia for a trial of assisted vaginal birth in theatre, keep an indwelling catheter after birth to prevent covert retention and remove it according to local protocol.

toxicities.incidence: In one trial involving women with assisted vaginal birth and/or a baby over 4 kg, a physiotherapist-delivered intervention reduced urinary incontinence at 3 months from 38.4% to 31.0%; the effect was smaller at 12 months.
prevention: Offer physiotherapy-directed strategies to lower the risk of urinary incontinence at 3 months; the guideline notes uncertainty about pelvic floor muscle exercise as treatment for incontinence in postnatal women.

toxicities.event: Maternal infection following assisted vaginal birth
toxicities.incidence: In the ANODE trial, confirmed or suspected infection occurred in 180 [11%] of 1619 women assigned amoxicillin and clavulanic acid versus 306 [19%] of 1606 assigned placebo (RR 0 58, 95% CI 0 49–0 69; P < 0 0001).
prevention: Recommend a single prophylactic intravenous dose of amoxicillin and clavulanic acid after assisted vaginal birth.
Maintain good hygiene and aseptic technique.

toxicities.event: Psychological morbidity and post-traumatic stress disorder (PTSD) symptoms
toxicities.incidence: In the UK national maternity survey in 2010, two or more PTSD-type symptoms at 3 months were reported by 25/359 [7%] women after forceps birth versus 93/3275 [3%] after unassisted birth (OR 4.89, 95% CI 2.68–8.9). The guideline describes the association between assisted vaginal birth and PTSD as complex and reports conflicting study findings.

management.actions: Review the indication for assisted birth, management of complications and options for future births, preferably with the obstetrician who performed the procedure.

management.severity: Traumatic birth with a wish to discuss the experience
management.actions: Offer advice and support, while also considering the effect on the birth partner; do not offer a single-session, high-intensity intervention focused explicitly on ‘reliving’ the trauma.
Offer referral to skilled professionals in accordance with NICE guidance on PTSD.

prevention: Shared decision making, effective communication and positive continuous support during labour and birth may reduce psychological morbidity.

The cited NICE intrapartum care guideline advises against routinely starting oxytocin in the second stage of labour and advises caution in multiparous women. An experienced obstetrician should assess a multiparous woman thoroughly before considering oxytocin at this stage.

toxicities.event: Increased pain when epidural analgesia is discontinued during pushing
toxicities.incidence: In the cited evidence, increased pain occurred in 22% when epidural analgesia was discontinued versus 6% when it was continued (RR 3.68, 95% CI 1.99–6.80).
prevention: Do not routinely stop epidural analgesia during pushing; evidence has not established that stopping it reduces assisted vaginal birth.

toxicities.event: Fetal head impaction at caesarean birth after failed forceps birth
recognition: A failed attempt at forceps birth preceding caesarean birth increases the risk of fetal head impaction.

management.severity: Caesarean birth following a failed forceps attempt
management.actions: Be prepared to disimpact the fetal head using recognised manoeuvres; the guideline describes disimpaction in advance of caesarean birth as good practice.

prophylaxis.recommendation: Recommend a single intravenous prophylactic dose of amoxicillin and clavulanic acid following assisted vaginal birth to significantly reduce confirmed or suspected maternal infection compared with placebo.
Reassess venous thromboembolism risk after assisted vaginal birth and prescribe thromboprophylaxis according to the risk factors identified.
Use good hygiene, aseptic technique and personal protective equipment to reduce infection and contamination.

Offer an indwelling catheter after birth to prevent covert urinary retention, removing it under local protocol. The guideline also specifies 6–12 hours after birth for women who had regional analgesia for a trial of assisted vaginal birth.
prophylaxis.target_population: Women who received regional analgesia for a trial of assisted vaginal birth in theatre

prophylaxis.recommendation: Offer physiotherapy-directed strategies to reduce urinary incontinence at 3 months.

Discuss mediolateral episiotomy during preparation for assisted vaginal birth and individualise its use rather than adopting a routine or restrictive policy. Evidence concerning prevention of OASI is stronger in nulliparous women and with forceps birth.
prophylaxis.target_population: Women preparing for assisted vaginal birth

prophylaxis.recommendation: Use shared decision making, good communication and positive continuous support during labour and birth; these measures have the potential to reduce psychological morbidity after birth.
prophylaxis.target_population: Women in labour and undergoing birth

infection_management.pathogen_or_syndrome: Confirmed or suspected maternal infection following assisted vaginal birth
infection_management.prevention: Recommend a single prophylactic intravenous dose of amoxicillin and clavulanic acid after assisted vaginal birth, together with good hygiene and aseptic technique.
In the ANODE trial, women receiving prophylactic amoxicillin and clavulanic acid were significantly less likely to experience perineal wound infection than those receiving placebo.
In a trial included in a Cochrane review, endometritis occurred in seven women given no antibiotic and none given prophylactic antibiotic (RR 0.07, 95% CI 0.00–1.21).

Maternal blood borne viral infection is not an absolute contraindication to assisted vaginal birth. The guideline advises avoiding difficult assisted birth with a greater chance of fetal abrasion or scalp trauma, as well as avoiding fetal scalp electrodes or blood sampling during labour.

therapies_index.name: continuous support during labour
approved_indications: Reducing the need for assisted vaginal birth during labour.
therapies_index.administration: Provide continuous support throughout labour.

therapies_index.name: epidural analgesia
approved_indications: Pain relief during labour.
therapies_index.administration: It may be initiated in either the latent or active phase of labour; routine discontinuation during pushing is not advised.
key_toxicities: It may increase the likelihood of assisted vaginal birth, although this is less likely with newer techniques.
Stopping it during pushing increases maternal pain.
It is associated with postpartum urinary retention.

therapies_index.name: patient-controlled epidural analgesia (PCEA)
approved_indications: Pain relief during labour.
therapies_index.administration: The woman controls epidural analgesia.

therapies_index.name: combined spinal–epidural
approved_indications: Regional analgesia during labour.

therapies_index.name: regional block
approved_indications: Analgesia for midpelvic or rotational assisted vaginal birth.
therapies_index.administration: Usually used for midpelvic or rotational birth.
monitoring: After a trial of assisted vaginal birth in theatre with regional analgesia, prevent unrecognised urinary retention with an indwelling catheter and monitor subsequent voiding volumes.

therapies_index.name: pudendal block
approved_indications: Possible analgesia for assisted vaginal birth, depending on urgency.

therapies_index.name: perineal block
approved_indications: Possible analgesia for low or outlet assisted vaginal birth.

therapies_index.name: upright or lateral positions
approved_indications: Reducing assisted vaginal birth in women without epidural analgesia during the second stage of labour.
therapies_index.administration: Adopt an upright or lateral position during the second stage of labour.

therapies_index.name: lying down lateral positions
approved_indications: Increasing spontaneous vaginal birth in women with epidural analgesia during the second stage of labour, compared with upright positions.
therapies_index.administration: Adopt a lying-down lateral position during the second stage of labour.

therapies_index.name: delayed pushing
approved_indications: Potentially reducing rotational and midpelvic assisted vaginal birth in nulliparous women with epidural analgesia.
therapies_index.administration: Delay pushing for 1–2 hours.

therapies_index.name: oxytocin
therapies_index.administration: Routine augmentation to reduce assisted vaginal birth in women with epidural analgesia is not supported by sufficient evidence. It should not routinely be started in the second stage of labour; an experienced obstetrician should assess a multiparous woman before considering its use then.
key_toxicities: A review reported a higher rate of uterine rupture among multiparous women in whom oxytocin had been started.

therapies_index.name: manual rotation
approved_indications: Correction of fetal malposition; it is also an option before direct traction forceps or vacuum extraction for rotational birth.
therapies_index.administration: Evidence is insufficient to recommend its routine prophylactic use in the second stage of labour to prevent assisted vaginal birth.

therapies_index.name: assisted vaginal birth
approved_indications: Maternal or fetal indications requiring assistance with birth, including suspected fetal compromise, lack of continuing progress, maternal exhaustion or distress, and medical indications to avoid the Valsalva manoeuvre.
therapies_index.administration: Use forceps or vacuum extraction only after full cervical dilatation and assessment of the safety criteria; choice of procedure depends on clinical circumstances and operator expertise.
key_toxicities: Maternal perineal and pelvic floor trauma.
Postpartum haemorrhage.
Neonatal traumatic injury, particularly with midpelvic, rotational or failed attempts.
Postpartum urinary retention.
monitoring: Assess maternal and fetal findings before the attempt.
Review the woman and baby after birth and document the procedure and postnatal plan.
Process and record paired cord blood samples after every attempt.

therapies_index.name: vacuum extraction
approved_indications: Assisted vaginal birth when vacuum is appropriate to the clinical circumstances and operator's skills.
therapies_index.administration: Avoid below 32 weeks of gestation and use cautiously between 32+0 and 36+0 weeks of gestation. In the majority of cases, use no more than three pulls to bring the head to the perineum; three further gentle pulls may ease it out. Stop if descent does not progress with moderate traction or after two ‘pop-offs’. Use rapid negative pressure application.
key_toxicities: Compared with forceps at preterm gestational ages, higher risk of subgaleal haemorrhage and scalp trauma.
Cephalhaematoma, retinal haemorrhage, neonatal scalp trauma and intracranial haemorrhage.
Maternal perineal trauma, obstetric anal sphincter injury (OASI) and postpartum haemorrhage.
Failed extraction is associated with increased neonatal morbidity.
monitoring: Check for progressive descent with each pull and count pulls and ‘pop-offs’.
After a failed attempt, alert the neonatologist and assess the baby for traumatic injury that may not be evident at birth.

therapies_index.name: soft cup vacuum extractors
approved_indications: Vacuum-assisted vaginal birth when the instrument is appropriate to the clinical circumstances.
key_toxicities: Higher failure rate but lower neonatal scalp-trauma incidence than rigid cups.

therapies_index.name: Kiwi TM OmniCup
approved_indications: Vacuum-assisted vaginal birth as evaluated in the cited studies.
key_toxicities: One cited trial reported more failures and more sequential instrument use than with a standard cup.

therapies_index.name: iCupTM
approved_indications: Vacuum-assisted vaginal birth as evaluated in a cited trial.
key_toxicities: The cited trial reported more failures with this disposable cup than with the metal vacuum.

therapies_index.name: Bird metal cup
approved_indications: Vacuum-assisted vaginal birth as evaluated in a cited trial.

therapies_index.name: forceps birth
approved_indications: Assisted vaginal birth when forceps are appropriate to the clinical circumstances and operator's skills.
Delivery of the after-coming head of the breech.
therapies_index.administration: Stop if application or handle approximation is difficult, descent does not progress with moderate traction, or birth is not imminent after three pulls with a correctly applied instrument.
key_toxicities: Maternal perineal trauma and obstetric anal sphincter injury (OASI).
Potential neonatal traumatic injury after a failed attempt.
A failed attempt increases the risk of fetal head impaction at a subsequent caesarean birth.
monitoring: Assess application, progressive descent and the number of pulls.
After failure, inform the neonatologist and assess the baby for traumatic injury that may not be immediately evident.

therapies_index.name: Kielland’s rotational forceps
approved_indications: Rotational assisted vaginal birth by an operator with specific expertise and training.
therapies_index.administration: Stop rotational forceps birth if gentle pressure does not readily achieve rotation.
key_toxicities: Additional risks include neonatal cervical spine injury.
monitoring: Assess whether rotation is achieved easily with gentle pressure.

therapies_index.name: direct traction forceps
approved_indications: Assisted vaginal birth following manual rotation when appropriate to the circumstances and operator's expertise.
therapies_index.administration: May follow manual rotation for a rotational birth.

therapies_index.name: rotational vacuum extraction
approved_indications: Rotational assisted vaginal birth by an experienced operator when clinically appropriate.
key_toxicities: A cited meta-analysis reported more failures and neonatal trauma than with Kielland’s forceps.

therapies_index.name: sequential use of instruments
therapies_index.administration: Avoid whenever possible; an inexperienced operator should not attempt it without direct supervision. Following failed vacuum extraction, weigh the risks of subsequent forceps against those of caesarean birth.
key_toxicities: Increased neonatal trauma and morbidity, including intracranial haemorrhage.
Increased obstetric anal sphincter injury (OASI).
monitoring: Inform the neonatologist when sequential instruments have been used and assess the baby for traumatic injury.

therapies_index.name: caesarean birth
approved_indications: Alternative to assisted vaginal birth in the second stage of labour, including when an attempted assisted vaginal birth fails.
therapies_index.administration: Ensure immediate access when an assisted vaginal birth has a higher anticipated risk of failure.
key_toxicities: Second-stage caesarean birth can involve significant maternal and perinatal morbidity.
Compared with completed assisted vaginal birth, it is associated with increased major obstetric haemorrhage, prolonged hospital stay and neonatal-unit admission.
Fetal head impaction is more likely after a failed forceps attempt.

therapies_index.name: mediolateral episiotomy
approved_indications: An individualised option at assisted vaginal birth; evidence for prevention of obstetric anal sphincter injury (OASI) is stronger in nulliparous women and with forceps birth.
therapies_index.administration: Discuss before assisted vaginal birth. If performed, initiate the cut at a 60 degree angle when the head distends the perineum.
key_toxicities: A cited UK prospective study associated episiotomy with increased postpartum haemorrhage.

therapies_index.name: amoxicillin and clavulanic acid
approved_indications: Prophylaxis after assisted vaginal birth to reduce confirmed or suspected maternal infection.
therapies_index.administration: A single intravenous prophylactic dose following assisted vaginal birth.

therapies_index.name: amoxicillin
approved_indications: A component of the prophylactic amoxicillin and clavulanic acid regimen after assisted vaginal birth.
therapies_index.administration: Given with clavulanic acid as a single intravenous prophylactic dose after assisted vaginal birth.

therapies_index.name: clavulanic acid
approved_indications: A component of the prophylactic amoxicillin and clavulanic acid regimen after assisted vaginal birth.
therapies_index.administration: Given with amoxicillin as a single intravenous prophylactic dose after assisted vaginal birth.

therapies_index.name: aseptic techniques
approved_indications: Reducing infection and contamination during obstetric care.
therapies_index.administration: Maintain good hygiene and use appropriate personal protective equipment.

therapies_index.name: thromboprophylaxis
approved_indications: Prevention of venous thromboembolism after assisted vaginal birth when indicated by reassessment of risk factors.
monitoring: Reassess venous thromboembolism risk after assisted vaginal birth.

therapies_index.name: nonsteroidal antiinflammatory drugs (NSAIDs)
approved_indications: Routine relief of postpartum perineal, vaginal and pelvic pain when there are no contraindications.
therapies_index.administration: Offer regularly after birth; the guideline discusses oral NSAIDs.

therapies_index.name: diclofenac
approved_indications: Relief of postpartum perineal pain.
therapies_index.administration: Oral administration is discussed.

therapies_index.name: ibuprofen
approved_indications: Relief of postpartum perineal pain.
therapies_index.administration: Oral administration is discussed.

therapies_index.name: paracetamol
approved_indications: Routine postpartum analgesia when there are no contraindications.
therapies_index.administration: Offer regularly after birth.

therapies_index.name: indwelling catheter
approved_indications: Prevention of covert urinary retention after a trial of assisted vaginal birth in theatre with regional analgesia.
therapies_index.administration: Keep in place after birth and remove under the local protocol; the guideline also specifies 6–12 hours after birth for women who received regional analgesia for a trial of assisted vaginal birth.
monitoring: Use fluid-balance charts after removal to check voiding volumes.

therapies_index.name: systematic intermittent bladder catheterisation
therapies_index.administration: A small, potentially biased ‘before and after’ study evaluated catheterisation at 2 hours post birth to prevent covert postpartum urinary retention.

therapies_index.name: physiotherapy-directed strategies
approved_indications: Reducing urinary incontinence at 3 months after assisted vaginal birth.
therapies_index.administration: Offer strategies directed by a physiotherapist.

therapies_index.name: pelvic floor muscle exercise
therapies_index.administration: The guideline reports uncertainty about its benefit for treating urinary incontinence in postnatal women.

therapies_index.name: single session, high-intensity psychological interventions
therapies_index.administration: Do not offer an intervention explicitly focused on ‘reliving’ the trauma.

therapies_index.name: psychological debriefing
therapies_index.administration: A cited review found little or no evidence of either a beneficial or harmful effect for preventing psychological trauma after childbirth.

special_populations.considerations: Delaying pushing may reduce the need for rotational or midpelvic assisted vaginal birth. Among women with epidural analgesia, lying down in a lateral position rather than remaining upright increases spontaneous vaginal birth.
special_populations.treatment_modifications: Delay pushing for 1–2 hours. Encourage a lying down lateral position during the second stage of labour.

special_populations.considerations: Upright or lateral positions during the second stage of labour reduce the need for assisted vaginal birth.
special_populations.treatment_modifications: Encourage upright or lateral positioning during the second stage of labour.

special_populations.considerations: A review reported a higher rate of uterine rupture among multiparous women who had started oxytocin. The guideline does not support routine oxytocin augmentation to reduce assisted vaginal birth among women with epidural analgesia.
special_populations.treatment_modifications: Use oxytocin cautiously in the second stage of labour; an experienced obstetrician should assess a multiparous woman thoroughly before considering it.

special_populations.considerations: At preterm gestational ages, vacuum extraction carries a higher risk of subgaleal haemorrhage and scalp trauma than forceps. Infants born below 32+0 weeks of gestation are particularly susceptible to cephalohaematoma, intracranial haemorrhage, subgaleal haemorrhage and neonatal jaundice.
special_populations.treatment_modifications: Avoid vacuum birth below 32 weeks of gestation and use it cautiously between 32+0 and 36+0 weeks of gestation.

special_populations.population: Fetuses with suspected bleeding disorders or a predisposition to fracture
special_populations.considerations: These conditions are relative contraindications to assisted vaginal birth. Delivering a fetal head that is deep in the pelvis by an abdominal route can also carry considerable risks.
special_populations.treatment_modifications: Involve an experienced obstetrician in decisions about exceptional indications, ideally with discussion documented before labour. Low forceps may be acceptable when a fetal bleeding disorder is suspected, but avoid vacuum extraction.

special_populations.population: Women with blood borne viral infections
special_populations.considerations: Maternal blood borne viral infection is not an absolute contraindication to assisted vaginal birth. Difficult procedures may increase the likelihood of fetal abrasion or scalp trauma.
special_populations.treatment_modifications: Avoid difficult assisted vaginal birth where possible, as well as fetal scalp electrodes and fetal blood sampling during labour.

special_populations.population: Women undergoing vacuum extraction after fetal blood sampling or fetal scalp electrode application
special_populations.considerations: A preceding fetal blood sampling procedure or fetal scalp electrode does not contraindicate vacuum extraction.

special_populations.population: Women with medical indications to avoid the Valsalva manoeuvre
special_populations.considerations: The guideline lists cardiac disease, hypertensive crisis, cerebral vascular disease or malformations, myasthenia gravis and spinal cord injury as medical indications that may warrant assisted vaginal birth. No indication is absolute; the decision requires individual clinical judgment.

special_populations.population: Women who received regional analgesia for a trial of assisted vaginal birth in theatre
special_populations.considerations: These women require precautions against covert postpartum urinary retention and asymptomatic bladder overfilling.
special_populations.treatment_modifications: Offer an indwelling catheter for 6–12 hours after birth, remove it according to local protocol, and then use fluid balance charts to assess voiding volumes.

special_populations.population: Women with persistent post-traumatic stress disorder (PTSD) symptoms after birth
special_populations.considerations: Psychological support after a traumatic birth should take account of the woman's wish to discuss her experience and the potential effect on her birth partner.
special_populations.treatment_modifications: At 1 month, refer women with persistent PTSD symptoms to skilled professionals in accordance with NICE guidance on PTSD. Do not offer a single high-intensity session explicitly focused on reliving the trauma.

special_populations.population: Women with a previous third- or fourth-degree perineal tear or ongoing pelvic floor morbidity
special_populations.considerations: A previous severe perineal tear, particularly when symptoms persist, may increase the risk of further anorectal damage in a subsequent birth.
special_populations.treatment_modifications: Individualise plans for future births and discuss recurrence risk and its implications.

artifacts.title: Table 3. Safety criteria for assisted vaginal birth
artifacts.source_heading: 4.4. What are the essential conditions for safe assisted vaginal birth?

rows: No more than 1/5 of the head is palpable abdominally, and in most cases none is palpable. The cervix is fully dilated and membranes are ruptured. Station is at the ischial spines or lower. Fetal head position is known. Caput and moulding are no greater than moderate (or +2). The pelvis is considered adequate.

Explain the procedure clearly, obtain informed consent and document it in the woman’s notes. Establish trust and obtain her cooperation. Ensure appropriate analgesia: usually a regional block for midpelvic or rotational birth; a pudendal block may be acceptable according to urgency; a perineal block may suffice for low or outlet birth. Empty the bladder, remove an indwelling catheter or deflate its balloon, and use aseptic technique.

The operator has the required knowledge, experience and skill. Provide suitable equipment, bed and lighting, with access to an operating theatre. For midpelvic birth, theatre facilities permit caesarean birth without delay; a senior obstetrician is present if the operator is inexperienced. Anticipate shoulder dystocia, perineal trauma and postpartum haemorrhage. Have personnel trained in neonatal resuscitation present.

artifacts.description: The table’s note defines moderate or +2 moulding as overlapping parietal bones that can readily be reduced; severe or +3 moulding describes irreducible overlap and indicates cephalopelvic disproportion.
artifacts.summary: This checklist covers examination findings, preparation of the woman, operator capability, facilities, contingency planning and neonatal support.

artifacts.title: Decision making for assisted vaginal birth
artifacts.source_heading: Appendix 3 Decision making for assisted vaginal birth
artifacts.description: Step 1: Confirm that the safety criteria for OVB are met. Step 2: Choose the place of birth. Consider a trial in theatre if 1/5th of the head is palpable abdominally, the head is mid-pelvic, rotation is needed or findings suggest CPD; continue in the labour room if the head is low-pelvic/outlet, rotation is unnecessary or easy, and there are no features of CPD. Step 3: Choose an instrument the operator or supervisor is competent to use and that is least likely to fail, aiming to avoid sequential instruments. Avoid vacuum-assisted birth at < 32 weeks gestation and use caution at 32–36 weeks. Step 4: Apply the instrument correctly. If correct application cannot be achieved, reassess engagement, position, station and asynclitism; less experienced operators seek another opinion, while an experienced operator reassesses and considers reapplication, another instrument or stopping. Stop if these measures do not achieve correct application. Step 5: Attempt rotation if indicated. If gentle rotation is unsuccessful, a senior obstetrician checks application and technique; stop if rotation remains unsuccessful. Birth in direct OP position may occur with vacuum or low-station forceps. Step 6: Apply traction. If descent does not progress, check application and reassess for cephalo-pelvic disproportion; less experienced operators seek another opinion, while an experienced operator may change instrument or traction direction. Stop if descent still cannot be achieved; stop vacuum-assisted birth after two ‘pop offs’. Step 7: Reassess after 3 pulls. Consider stopping vacuum-assisted birth if the head has not reached the pelvic floor, allowing a maximum 3 gentle pulls to ease birth over the perineum; consider stopping forceps birth if the head is not crowning and birth is not imminent. Step 8: After a failed OVB attempt, consider forceps following failed vacuum only if the vertex is at a low station. Weigh fetal trauma and OASI with sequential instruments against maternal morbidity from second-stage caesarean birth and the risk of fetal head impaction. Inform the neonatologist about increased neonatal morbidity risk, complete the OVB proforma and discuss the birth with the mother, partner and family.
artifacts.summary: The flowchart traces preparation, choice of setting and instrument, checks during application and traction, stopping decisions and actions after a failed attempt.
artifacts.clinical_relevance: It provides decision points for recognising poor progress, limiting unsuccessful attempts and planning subsequent maternal and neonatal care.
