document_sections.heading: Executive summary
document_sections.content: The summary recommends continuous labour support (A); counselling that epidural analgesia may increase assisted vaginal birth, although newer techniques may lessen this effect (A); explaining that starting epidural analgesia in latent rather than active labour does not increase that risk (A); upright or lateral second-stage positions without epidural analgesia (A); lying lateral rather than upright positions with epidural analgesia (A); and delayed pushing for 1–2 hours in nulliparous women with epidural analgesia, which may reduce rotational and midpelvic intervention (B). Epidural analgesia should not routinely be stopped during pushing because pain increases without evidence of fewer assisted births (A). Evidence is insufficient to favour a particular regional analgesia technique (A), routine oxytocin augmentation with epidural analgesia (A), or routine prophylactic manual rotation of second-stage fetal malposition (B) for reducing assisted birth. The summary calls for standard classification (D), individual clinical judgment because no indication is absolute (D), and careful assessment, communication and procedural expertise (D). Suspected fetal bleeding disorders or fracture susceptibility are relative contraindications (P); maternal blood-borne viral infection is not an absolute contraindication (D); and prior fetal blood sampling or scalp-electrode placement does not contraindicate vacuum extraction (B). Compared with forceps, preterm vacuum extraction carries more subgaleal haemorrhage and scalp trauma; avoid it below 32 weeks and exercise caution between 32+0 and 36+0 weeks (C). Assess fetal head position with ultrasound when examination leaves uncertainty (B); evidence does not support routine abdominal or perineal ultrasound for station, flexion or descent (C). Discuss assisted birth antenatally, obtain and document verbal consent for birth-room procedures, and obtain written consent for a theatre trial after comparing midpelvic or rotational assisted birth with second-stage caesarean birth (P). Appropriately skilled operators should perform or attend procedures (D); trainees should gain spontaneous-birth experience, receive supervised theoretical, simulation and clinical training, and demonstrate competence before independent practice (P). Reserve complex procedures for experienced operators or direct supervision (D), with an operator competent in midpelvic birth present from the outset for rotational or midpelvic attempts (D). Most non-rotational low-pelvic and outlet procedures can take place in a birth room (C); higher-risk attempts require immediate access to caesarean birth (C). Select instruments according to circumstances and skill (P): vacuum more often fails with a single instrument, whereas forceps more often cause maternal perineal trauma (A); soft vacuum cups fail more often but cause less neonatal scalp trauma (A). Experienced operators may choose Kielland’s rotational forceps, manual rotation followed by direct traction forceps or vacuum, or rotational vacuum extraction (C). Stop vacuum extraction without progressive descent, after two ‘pop-offs’, or when reassessment after the first two minimally effective pulls indicates that the approach should change; ordinarily bring the head to the perineum within three pulls, allowing three further gentle pulls for delivery (P). Rapid application of negative pressure shortens vacuum procedures without changing maternal or neonatal outcomes (P). Sequential instruments increase neonatal trauma (B) and OASI (C); inform neonatology after failed vacuum extraction or sequential use (P). Stop forceps when placement or handle approximation is difficult, descent fails, gentle rotation cannot be achieved, or birth is not imminent after three pulls (B); reassess poor early descent, inform neonatology after failure, and anticipate fetal-head impaction if caesarean birth follows (P). Discuss mediolateral episiotomy (P), individualise its use because robust evidence does not establish a routine or restrictive policy, and recognise stronger OASI-prevention evidence for nulliparous women and forceps birth (B); make the cut at a 60 degree angle as the head distends the perineum (B). After assisted birth, recommend one prophylactic intravenous dose of amoxicillin and clavulanic acid (A), maintain hygiene and asepsis (P), reassess thromboembolism risk (D), and offer regular NSAIDs and paracetamol unless contraindicated (A). Explain urinary-retention risk, record the first void, measure residual urine when retention is suspected, use an indwelling catheter after a theatre trial with regional analgesia according to local removal policy, and offer physiotherapy-directed measures against incontinence at 3 months (P, C, P, P and B, respectively). Shared decisions, communication and support may reduce psychological morbidity; review the birth before discharge, support women wishing to discuss trauma, and do not offer a single high-intensity session centred on reliving it (P). Refer persistent PTSD symptoms at 1 month under NICE guidance (D). Explain the high chance of spontaneous vaginal birth subsequently (B) and individualise care after third- or fourth-degree tears or persistent pelvic-floor problems (P). Record assessment, decisions, procedure and postnatal plans in a standardised proforma; process paired cord samples after every attempt; and report specified serious outcomes (P). Following serious events, prioritise continuing care, practise candour, participate in reporting and review, and provide support to families and staff (P).

document_sections.heading: 1. Purpose and scope
document_sections.content: The guideline addresses evidence-based use of forceps and vacuum extraction for rotational and non-rotational assisted vaginal birth, including indications, technique and governance. To manage the range of clinical situations safely, obstetricians should become competent with both instruments for non-rotational birth and with at least one specialist rotational technique.

document_sections.heading: 2. Introduction and background
document_sections.content: Vacuum and forceps assist birth for maternal or fetal reasons. In the UK, assisted vaginal birth accounts for between 10% and 15% of births and nearly one in every three births among nulliparous women; rates are lower in midwifery-led settings. Increasing second-stage caesarean birth may reflect concern about assisted-birth morbidity or declining procedural skills. Most properly performed procedures by trained staff are safe for mother and baby. Compared with first-birth caesarean, successful assisted vaginal birth makes an uncomplicated vaginal birth in a later pregnancy much more likely. Rare severe complications include subgaleal and intracranial haemorrhage, skull fracture and spinal-cord injury; these may cause perinatal death and are more likely after midpelvic, rotational or unsuccessful attempts. Late second-stage caesarean birth can itself cause substantial maternal and perinatal morbidity, making the choice complex. Developments since the 2011 guideline include the Montgomery ruling’s emphasis on informed consent and criminal convictions following serious deficiencies in care associated with a patient’s death. Reports to RCOG of neonatal deaths linked to birth trauma also informed the updated safety guidance.

document_sections.heading: 3. Identification and assessment of evidence
document_sections.content: Development followed standard RCOG Green-top Guidelines (GTGs) methods. Searches covered the Cochrane Library, including its systematic-review, DARE and CENTRAL databases, EMBASE, MEDLINE and Trip, and relevant guidelines in the National Guideline Clearinghouse and NICE Evidence Search. Eligible literature was published through May 2019; searches combined Medical Subject Headings and keywords concerning forceps, manual rotation and assisted or operative birth, and were restricted to human studies and English-language papers. The full strategies appear in Appendix S1 and S2. Recommendations draw on available evidence where possible; areas without adequate evidence are identified as good practice points. Appendix 1 explains evidence assessment and recommendation grading.

document_sections.heading: 4.1. Can assisted vaginal birth be avoided?
document_sections.content: The guideline recommends continuous labour support (A). A synthesis of 26 trials involving n = 15 858 associated such support with more spontaneous vaginal births (RR 1.08, 95% CI 1.04–1.12) and fewer assisted vaginal births (RR 0.90, 95% CI 0.85–0.96), particularly when the supporter was not staff (Evidence level 1++). Counsel women that epidural analgesia may increase assisted vaginal birth, though newer approaches may be less likely to do so (A). Against non-epidural methods, a review found more assisted births with epidural analgesia (23 trials; n = 7935; OR 1.42, 95% CI 1.28–1.57) but better pain relief (3 trials; n = 1166; mean difference in maternal perception of pain –3.36; 95% CI – 5.41 to –1.31). A post hoc subgroup analysis did not reproduce the increase in assisted birth and suggested that lower local-analgesic concentrations or PCEA may differ from older approaches (Evidence level 1++). Inform women that latent-phase rather than active-phase initiation does not increase assisted-birth risk (A); among nulliparous women, 6 trials involving n = 15 399 found RR 0.96, 95% CI 0.89–1.05 (Evidence level 1+). Without epidural analgesia, encourage upright or lateral second-stage positions (A); compared with supine or lithotomy positions, a review reported fewer assisted births (21 trials; n = 6481; RR 0.75, 95% CI 0.66 to –0.86; Evidence level 1+). With epidural analgesia, encourage lying lateral rather than upright positions (A). In a randomised trial of 3236 nulliparous women receiving low-dose epidural analgesia, spontaneous birth occurred in 35.2% (548/1556) of the upright group versus 41.1% (632/1537) of the lying-down group (adjusted RR 0.86, 95% CI 0.78–0.94); the reported absolute advantage for lying down was 5.9%, with number needed to treat 17; 95% CI 11–40 (Evidence level 1+). Recommend delaying pushing for 1–2 hours in nulliparous women with epidural analgesia because it may reduce rotational and midpelvic assisted birth (B). One meta-analysis reported RR 0.59, 95% CI 0.36–0.98 for delay of 1 to 2 hours or until a strong urge to push; a later high-quality-study analysis found a smaller, statistically nonsignificant effect (Evidence level 1++). Do not routinely stop epidural analgesia for pushing (A): evidence did not establish fewer assisted births (23% versus 28%; RR 0.84, 95% CI 0.61–1.15), whereas pain increased (22% versus 6%; RR 3.68, 95% CI 1.99–6.80; Evidence level 1++). Evidence is insufficient to recommend one regional analgesia technique to prevent assisted birth (A). Combined spinal–epidural versus standard epidural analgesia showed no difference (19 trials; n = 2658; OR 0.82, 95% CI 0.67–1.00); comparisons of PCEA with continuous infusion, including nine studies with 641 women and a trial of 126 women, also found comparable obstetric or normal-birth outcomes (Evidence level 1+). Evidence is insufficient to recommend routine oxytocin augmentation for women receiving epidural analgesia as prevention (A). A review of oxytocin from 6 cm dilatation found no significant assisted-birth reduction (two studies; n = 319; RR 0.88, 95% CI 0.72–1.08) and reported more uterine rupture among multiparous recipients. The cited NICE guidance advises against routinely starting oxytocin in the second stage and calls for caution in multiparous women; an experienced obstetrician should assess such a woman thoroughly before considering it (Evidence level 1+). Evidence is also insufficient to recommend routine prophylactic manual rotation of second-stage malposition for this purpose (B). A retrospective cohort linked manual rotation to fewer caesareans (9% versus 41%; P < 0.001); among 731 rotated women, none had cord prolapse, and neonatal trauma and acidaemia did not differ by attempted rotation. A prospective cohort of 172 attempts reported 90% success and fewer operative births (23% versus 39%; OR 0.52, 95% CI 0.28–0.95). A pilot RCT of 30 women reported a similar assisted-birth rate, while another RCT of 65 women found a shorter second stage (65 minutes versus 82 minutes; P = 0.04); neither trial reported rotation-related adverse effects. Larger RCTs are needed to establish whether early prophylactic rotation reduces operative birth (Evidence level 1–).

document_sections.heading: 4.2. How should assisted vaginal birth be defined?
document_sections.content: Use a consistent classification to support safety, communication and outcome audit (D). Classification requires systematic abdominal and vaginal examination. Marked caput can falsely suggest a lower vertex. Usually the head is not palpable abdominally; with a deflexed occipito-posterior position, however, up to one-fifth may remain palpable when the skull is at station 0 cm or lower. Table 1 sets out the classification developed for an earlier edition and incorporated into ACOG guidance: outlet birth involves visible scalp without separating the labia, skull at the perineum and rotation not exceeding 45°; low birth involves a skull at station + 2 cm but not at the perineum; and mid birth involves no more than one-fifth of the head palpable abdominally and the leading skull point at station 0 or + 1 cm. Low and mid categories distinguish non-rotational movement ≤ 45° from rotational movement > 45°.

document_sections.heading: 4.3. When should assisted vaginal birth be recommended/contraindicated?
document_sections.content: No indication is absolute; decisions require individual clinical judgment (D). Table 2 summarises fetal, maternal and combined indications. Suspected fetal compromise may involve pathological cardiotocography, an abnormal fetal blood sample or thick meconium. For absent continuing progress across active and passive second-stage labour, its guide times are 3 hours with regional analgesia or 2 hours without it for nulliparous women, and 2 hours or 1 hour, respectively, for parous women. Maternal exhaustion, distress and medical reasons to avoid Valsalva also feature; fetal and maternal indications may coexist. A retrospective cohort of 15 759 nulliparous women reported significantly greater maternal morbidity after 3 hours and a further increase after 4 hours, without evidence of increased neonatal morbidity in its setting of surveillance and timely intervention. These times guide, rather than dictate, intervention; compare continued pushing, assisted birth and second-stage caesarean birth, and consider a lower intervention threshold when factors coexist. Medical examples include cardiac disease, hypertensive crisis, cerebral vascular disease or malformations, myasthenia gravis and spinal-cord injury. Neither forceps nor vacuum should be used before complete cervical dilatation; forceps can deliver an after-coming breech head, while vacuum is contraindicated for face presentation. Suspected fetal bleeding disorders, including alloimmune thrombocytopenia, or fracture predisposition, including osteogenesis imperfecta, are relative contraindications (P). Because abdominal delivery of a deeply positioned head also carries risk, experienced obstetricians should decide exceptional cases and ideally discuss and record the plan before labour. Low forceps may be acceptable for suspected fetal bleeding disorders, but avoid vacuum (Evidence level 4). Maternal blood-borne viral infection is not an absolute contraindication (D). Surveillance of 251 assisted births in HIV-positive women found one infant with confirmed infection at 18 months; maternal characteristics suggested transmission might not have occurred intrapartum. Avoid difficult assisted birth likely to abrade the fetus or injure its scalp, as well as scalp electrodes or intrapartum blood sampling (Evidence level 3). Prior fetal blood sampling or scalp-electrode application does not contraindicate vacuum extraction (B). Two case studies reported fetal haemorrhage in this setting, but two randomised forceps-versus-vacuum trials reported no bleeding (Evidence level 1+ and 3). Compared with forceps at preterm gestations, vacuum carries greater subgaleal-haemorrhage and scalp-trauma risk; avoid vacuum below 32 weeks and use caution between 32+0 and 36+0 weeks (C). In a retrospective study of 5064 vacuum and 432 forceps births at 32+0 to 36+6 weeks, vacuum was associated with subgaleal haemorrhage of 0.16% versus 0%, intracranial haemorrhage of 0.12% versus 0%, and scalp trauma of 9.8% versus 6.3%. A Swedish registry reported vacuum use in 5.7% of preterm births and, versus spontaneous vaginal birth, intracranial haemorrhage of 1.5%; aOR 1.84, 95% CI 1.09–1.32, and extracranial haemorrhage of 0.64%; aOR 4.48, 95% CI 2.84–7.07. Follow-up of 266 vacuum-born babies reported comparable long-term neurological outcomes. Below 32+0 weeks, vacuum is not recommended because of susceptibility to cephalohaematoma, intracranial or subgaleal haemorrhage and neonatal jaundice (Evidence level 2+).

document_sections.heading: 4.4. What are the essential conditions for safe assisted vaginal birth?
document_sections.content: Safe practice requires clinical assessment, clear communication with the woman and staff, planning, and expertise with the selected procedure (D; Evidence level 4). Table 3 organises safety criteria into examination and preparation of the woman and team. Examination establishes a head ≤ 1/5 palpable abdominally, complete dilatation, ruptured membranes, station at or below the ischial spines, known head position, adequate pelvis, and caput and moulding no worse than moderate or +2. At +2, overlapping parietal bones remain reducible; at +3, overlap is irreducible and indicates cephalopelvic disproportion. Preparation includes explanation and documented consent, cooperation, appropriate analgesia, an emptied bladder, removal of an indwelling catheter or deflation of its balloon, and asepsis. A regional block is usual for midpelvic or rotational birth; depending on urgency, pudendal block may suffice, while perineal block may suffice for low or outlet birth. The team needs an appropriately skilled operator, equipment and theatre access, a backup plan enabling prompt caesarean birth for midpelvic attempts, senior attendance when an inexperienced obstetrician operates, readiness for shoulder dystocia, perineal trauma and postpartum haemorrhage, and staff trained in neonatal resuscitation.

document_sections.heading: 4.5. Does ultrasound have a role in assessment prior to assisted vaginal birth?
document_sections.content: Clinicians should recognise that ultrasound determines fetal head position more reliably than clinical examination (A); use it before assisted birth when examination leaves positional uncertainty (B). In a multicentre RCT, erroneous position diagnosis occurred in 4/257 [1.6%] with ultrasound versus 52/257 [20.2%] with standard care (OR 0.06, 95% CI 0.02–0.19; P < 0.001). More accurate diagnosis is important but ultrasound itself did not reduce morbidity. Another trial, assessing position from 8 cm dilatation, found more caesareans with ultrasound than vaginal examination (7.8% versus 4.9%; RR 1.60, 95% CI 1.12–2.28), without a significant assisted-birth difference (25.8% versus 22.2%; RR 1.16, 95% CI 0.99–1.37; Evidence level 1+). A UK-and-Ireland survey identified positional diagnostic errors across experience levels; operators using abdominal ultrasound should be trained in fetal-position identification (Evidence level 1+). Evidence and technical standardisation are insufficient to recommend routine abdominal or perineal ultrasound to assess station, flexion or descent in the second stage (C; Evidence level 2+).

document_sections.heading: 4.6. What type of consent is required prior to attempting assisted vaginal birth?
document_sections.content: Provide antenatal information about assisted birth, particularly in a first pregnancy, and ideally discuss stated preferences or restrictions with an experienced obstetrician before labour (P). For birth-room procedures, obtain verbal consent and document the discussion (P). For midpelvic or rotational procedures, compare assisted birth with second-stage caesarean birth in light of individual circumstances and operator skill; obtain written consent for a theatre trial (P). The 2015 Montgomery determination established a duty to explain material intervention risks and reasonable alternatives. Antenatal discussion is important because emergency decisions late in labour may limit a woman’s ability to absorb details; it should include means of reducing intervention and comparative morbidity. Respect and discuss her birth plan, including instrument objections; account for pain, exhaustion or drugs, provide information between contractions, convey risk in a time-sensitive manner, and record assessment, reasons and consent (Evidence level 4). A UK prospective cohort of 393 women transferred to theatre in the second stage reported more maternal haemorrhage and neonatal-unit admission after caesarean birth, but more pelvic-floor morbidity and neonatal trauma after assisted birth. Pelvic-floor morbidity was three-fold higher at 6 weeks after assisted birth, with attenuation at 1 and 3 years; later vaginal birth occurred in 80% versus 30%, and neurodevelopment at 5 years did not differ (Evidence level 2+). Two retrospective neonatal-outcome comparisons yielded similar complications in an Irish study and poorer outcomes after caesarean in an Israeli study; secondary analysis of a US trial involving 990 nulliparous women found comparable adverse neonatal outcomes after forceps, vacuum and caesarean birth. Canadian studies conflicted: one retrospective study found greater severe trauma after midpelvic assisted birth, particularly with sequential instruments, whereas a prospective cohort found no difference in severe maternal or neonatal morbidity between midpelvic and low assisted birth (Evidence level 2+). Obstetricians are directed to RCOG Consent Advice No. 11 and Clinical Governance Advice No. 6a (Evidence level 2+).

document_sections.heading: 5.1. Who should perform assisted vaginal birth?
document_sections.content: The operator performing or attending assisted birth must be able to assess the woman, finish the procedure and manage complications (D). Trainees should first gain expertise in spontaneous vaginal birth, then receive theoretical, simulation and directly supervised clinical training with vacuum and forceps, and demonstrate competence before practising without supervision (P). Complex births require an experienced operator or direct supervision by one (D). Inadequate training contributes to adverse outcomes (Evidence level 2+). The intended procedure resembles spontaneous birth while expediting delivery with minimal maternal or neonatal morbidity; knowledge of pelvic and fetal-head anatomy and normal labour is foundational. Training resources include guidelines, skills taxonomies, manuals and StratOG; the woman should know when a trainee works under direct supervision (Evidence level 4). Ideally, assess competence with the RCOG OSATS form. No evidence establishes a minimum number of supervised procedures; competence may vary individually. Units should ideally assign trainers, and courses may help maintain expertise (Evidence level 4). Practitioner audit, statistical process-control charts for vacuum performance and chignon position for cup-placement monitoring have been explored; better collection and constructive feedback methods require development (Evidence level 3). Midpelvic and rotational procedures require greater clinical and technical skill and carry more maternal and neonatal morbidity. Inexperienced operators’ initially unsuccessful attempts have been associated with serious neonatal trauma, reinforcing training and supervision before independent practice (Evidence level 2+).

document_sections.heading: 5.2. Who should supervise assisted vaginal birth?
document_sections.content: An experienced operator competent with midpelvic births should supervise every rotational or midpelvic attempt from its outset (D). If success is uncertain, such an operator should review the decision, instrument and setting. For a theatre trial, an experienced operator should attend or be immediately available when the trainee has not been signed off as competent (Evidence level 4). An Irish prospective series of 597 assisted births found no evidence that daytime versus nighttime birth was associated with adverse perinatal outcomes despite off-site consultant support at night; senior attendance was policy for theatre attempts. An Israeli retrospective study associated nighttime vacuum birth with greater neonatal morbidity but did not report staffing (Evidence level 2+). US studies associated designated, experienced teaching staff with improved trainee forceps outcomes and senior daytime supervision with more forceps and fewer caesarean births; the latter change was not evident at night (Evidence level 2+).

document_sections.heading: 5.3. Where should assisted vaginal birth take place?
document_sections.content: Most non-rotational low-pelvic and outlet procedures have little likelihood of failure and can safely occur in a birth room (C). Treat attempts with greater failure risk as trials in a setting permitting immediate caesarean birth (C). In a Scottish study of 1021 term singleton operative births for fetal distress, labour-room non-rotational low-pelvic forceps and vacuum birth achieved a decision-to-delivery target of 15 minutes without assisted-birth failure (Evidence level 2+). Factors associated with failure include maternal BMI greater than 30, short stature, estimated fetal weight greater than 4 kg or a clinically large baby, head circumference above the 95th percentile, occipito-posterior position, midpelvic birth and one-fifth of the head palpable abdominally. Failure is particularly more likely at station 0 or when rotation is needed; head circumference above the 95th percentile has shown a stronger association with unplanned caesarean or assisted birth than birth weight. Preliminary intrapartum sonography findings require further study (Evidence level 2+). Theatre allows prompt rescue for higher-risk trials, and available evidence shows little added maternal or neonatal morbidity from a failed attempt versus immediate caesarean when rescue is immediate. Among 3189 US women, adverse neonatal outcomes after failed attempts were associated with non-reassuring fetal-heart recordings; removing those cases removed the observed association between failure and adverse outcome (Evidence level 2+). Transfer delays must also be considered. A study of 229 operative births reported decision-to-delivery intervals of 20 minutes in the birth room and 59 minutes in theatre; a study of 1021 term singleton operative births for fetal distress found a labour-room target of 15 minutes versus an average of 30 minutes in theatre. Neither study found statistically significant neonatal-outcome differences between shorter and longer intervals. Balance labour-room failure risk against transfer time (Evidence level 2+).

document_sections.heading: 5.4. What instruments should be used for assisted vaginal birth?
document_sections.content: Choose the instrument according to clinical circumstances and operator skill (P). Compared with forceps, vacuum is more likely to fail as a single instrument, whereas forceps more often cause maternal perineal injury (A). Soft vacuum cups fail more often but cause less neonatal scalp trauma (A). Experienced operators should undertake rotational birth, selecting among Kielland’s rotational forceps, manual rotation followed by direct traction forceps or vacuum, and rotational vacuum extraction (C). A Cochrane review of 10 trials involving 2923 women underlies Table 4 (Evidence level 1++). Relative to forceps, its listed vacuum outcomes are greater failure to achieve vaginal birth (OR 1.7; 95% CI 1.3–2.2), cephalhaematoma (OR 2.4; 95% CI 1.7–3.4), retinal haemorrhage (OR 2.0; 95% CI 1.3–3.0) and maternal worry about the baby (OR 2.2; 95% CI 1.2–3.9); less significant perineal and vaginal trauma (OR 0.4; 95% CI 0.3–0.5); and no greater likelihood of caesarean birth (OR 0.6; 95% CI 0.3–1.0), low 5 min Apgar scores (OR 1.7; 95% CI 1.0–2.8) or phototherapy (OR 1.1; 95% CI 0.7–1.8). Three device trials reported vacuum failure rates from 17% to 36%. Among 194 women, Kiwi TM OmniCup failed in 34% versus 21% with a standard cup (aOR 2.3, 95% CI 1.01–5.0), with sequential-instrument rates of 22% versus 10%. Among 404 women, occipito-anterior failure was 26% versus 17% (RR 1.55, 95% CI 1.00–2.40); fetal malposition made vacuum failure three to four times more likely. In a French trial of 666 women, disposable iCupTM failed more often than metal vacuum (35.6% versus 7.1%; P < 0.0001). A Papua New Guinea trial reported failures of 2/100 with Kiwi Omnicup and 6/100 with the Bird metal cup; a cohort of 1000 Kiwi TM OmniCup births reported 12.9% failure (Evidence level 1+). A review of nine RCTs involving 1368 women found that soft versus rigid cups increased failure (OR 1.6, 95% CI 1.2–2.3) but reduced neonatal scalp trauma (OR 0.4, 95% CI 0.3–0.6; Evidence level 1++). Serious maternal complications have included cervical tears with vacuum and uterine rupture with forceps. Both instruments are associated with more episiotomy, pelvic-floor tears, levator ani avulsion and OASI than spontaneous birth; associated symptoms include pain, dyspareunia and urinary or bowel incontinence. A longitudinal cohort nested within an episiotomy-policy RCT found pelvic-floor morbidity often at least as prevalent in the third trimester as after birth, suggesting that some subsequent morbidity may not be caused by the procedure. A forceps-versus-vacuum trial found no significant urinary or bowel-function difference at 5 years (Evidence level 2+). Intracranial and subgaleal neonatal haemorrhage can be life-threatening. Among 583 340 liveborn singleton infants of nulliparous women, subdural or cerebral haemorrhage rates were 1 in 860 after vacuum, 1 in 664 after forceps and 1 in 954 after intrapartum caesarean birth, without significant differences among these modes; exposure to both instruments increased the rate to 1 in 256 (Evidence level 1+). Risk information lists episiotomy at 50–60% with vacuum and more than or equal to 90% with forceps; significant vulvo-vaginal tears at 10% and 20%; OASI at 1–4% and 8–12%; and postpartum haemorrhage at 10–40% with vacuum and forceps. Urinary or bowel incontinence is common at 6 weeks and improves over time. Perinatal estimates are cephalhaematoma, predominantly vacuum, 1–12%; facial or scalp lacerations, both instruments, 10%; retinal haemorrhage, more common with vacuum, 17–38%; jaundice or hyperbilirubinaemia, both instruments, 5–15%; subgaleal haemorrhage, predominantly vacuum, 3 to 6 in 1000; and intracranial haemorrhage, both instruments, 5 to 15 in 10 000. Cervical-spine injury is rare and mainly linked to Kiellands rotational forceps; skull fracture and facial-nerve palsy are rare and mainly linked to forceps; fetal death is very rare. The ‘Od on’ device cannot be recommended routinely before full evaluation (Evidence level 2+). No RCT has compared rotational techniques. Kielland’s forceps require specialist training and may cause cervical-spine injury. A meta-analysis of 23 studies found less failure (RR 0.32, 95% CI 0.14–0.76) and neonatal trauma (RR 0.62, 95% CI 0.46– 0.85) with Kielland’s forceps than rotational vacuum. In a prospective cohort of 381 rotational births, serious adverse outcomes were few and maternal and perinatal outcomes comparable, while sequential use was less frequent with manual rotation or direct forceps than rotational vacuum (0.6% versus 36.9%; OR 0.01, 95% CI 0.002–0.09). In a theatre cohort, attempted forceps more often achieved vaginal birth than attempted vacuum (63% versus 48%; P < 0.01). Retrospective studies report Kielland’s-forceps success of 90–95% with low morbidity under experienced operators (Evidence level 2+). Further training in rotational skills is encouraged, particularly for trainees taking advanced labour-ward modules.

document_sections.heading: 5.5. When should vacuum-assisted birth be discontinued and how should a discontinued vacuum procedure be managed?
document_sections.content: Stop if moderate traction with each pull of a correctly placed cup does not produce progressive descent (P). In most cases, bring the head to the perineum with no more than three pulls; up to three further gentle pulls may deliver it over the perineum (P). With minimal descent after the first two pulls, consider poor placement, mistaken position or cephalopelvic disproportion. Less experienced operators should stop and seek another opinion; experienced operators should reassess and change course or discontinue (P). Stop after two ‘pop-offs’; less experienced operators should seek senior help after one (P). Rapid negative-pressure application is recommended because it shortens the procedure without changing maternal or neonatal outcomes (P). Sequential instruments increase neonatal trauma: balance forceps after failed vacuum against caesarean after failed vacuum (B). Tell the neonatologist about failed vacuum or sequential use to support neonatal care (P), and recognise the increased OASI risk with sequential use (C). Procedural guidance largely rests on specialist consensus. Vacca recommends up to three pulls to reach the pelvic floor and up to three further pulls over the perineum, episiotomy for a very resistant perineum, and not treating ‘pop-off’ as a safety mechanism because detachment under full traction may injure fetal vessels. A skills taxonomy advises completion within three to four contractions (Evidence level 4). A study nested in an RCT of 478 nulliparous women associated suboptimal placement with neonatal trauma (OR 4.25, 95% CI 1.85–9.72), sequential instruments (OR 3.99, 95% CI 1.94–8.23) and caesarean for failed assisted birth (OR 3.81, 95% CI 1.10–13.2; Evidence level 2+). A cohort of 3594 low or outlet vacuum births found 5.8% failure; two ‘pop-offs’ versus none increased failure (OR 3.58, 95% CI 2.22–5.77), while application for more than 12 minutes versus 0–2 minutes increased composite adverse neonatal outcome (OR 6.9, 95% CI 3.58–11.79; Evidence level 2+). A review of two RCTs involving 754 women found no significant differences in detachments, low Apgar scores, scalp injury, cephalhaematoma or traction count between rapid pressure and increments of 0–2 kg per 2 minutes until 0–8 kg; the larger trial of 660 participants found a median application-to-birth difference of –4.4 minutes (95% CI –4.8 to –4.0; Evidence level 1+). Follow manufacturer guidance when available. Low or outlet forceps after failed vacuum may avoid difficult caesarean, which is associated with more major haemorrhage, longer admission and more neonatal-unit admission than completed assisted birth (Evidence level 2++). Conversely, intracranial haemorrhage was reported in 1 in 256 births exposed to two instruments versus 1 in 334 after failed forceps followed by caesarean. A US analysis of 12 014 739 live births found that sequential vacuum and forceps versus forceps alone increased mechanical ventilation (aOR 2.22, 95% CI 1.24– 3.97), as well as intracranial and retinal haemorrhage and feeding difficulty (Evidence level 2+). Follow-up of 7987 babies after attempted vacuum, including 245 (3.1%) failed attempts, found no increased long-term neurological morbidity through 18 years (Evidence level 2+). Neonatal staff should watch for initially occult injury after failure, multiple pulls, detachments or multiple instruments. Among 1360 UK nulliparous women, sequential use versus forceps alone was associated with OASI of 17.4% versus 8.4% (OR 2.1, 95% CI 1.2–33). A US series of 760 sequential births found greater risk than vacuum alone (OR 2.77, 95% CI 2.36–3.26) or forceps alone (OR 1.39, 95% CI 1.08-1.64; Evidence level 2+). Avoid sequential use where possible and do not let an inexperienced operator attempt it without direct supervision.

document_sections.heading: 5.6. When should attempted forceps birth be discontinued and how should a discontinued forceps procedure be managed?
document_sections.content: Stop if forceps placement or handle approximation is difficult or moderate traction produces no progressive descent (B). Stop rotational forceps if gentle pressure does not readily achieve rotation (B). Stop if birth is not imminent after three pulls with correctly applied forceps by an experienced operator (B). After minimal descent on the first one or two pulls, assess placement, position and cephalopelvic disproportion; less experienced operators should stop and seek a second opinion, whereas experienced operators should reassess, change strategy or discontinue (P). Inform neonatology after a failed attempt because neonatal morbidity may occur (P). If caesarean follows failed forceps, anticipate fetal-head impaction and prepare recognised disimpaction manoeuvres (P). In a cohort of 393 rotational or midpelvic attempts, more than three pulls increased neonatal trauma and special-care admission; risk rose further if failed assisted birth ended in caesarean. At 5 years, neurodevelopment did not differ between assisted and caesarean births; two cerebral-palsy cases occurred after caesarean and were not causally linked to delivery mode (Evidence level 2+). Among 1731 low or outlet forceps births, failure was 4.9%; 3 or more pulls versus one increased failure (OR 3.24, 95% CI 1.59–6.61), and application longer than 12 minutes versus 0–2 minutes increased composite adverse neonatal outcome (OR 5.37, 95% CI 1.49–19.32; Evidence level 2+). A study nested within an RCT of 478 nulliparous women found suboptimal placement more often with forceps than vacuum and associated it with neonatal trauma (OR 4.25, 95% CI 1.85–9.72) and caesarean after failed assisted birth (OR 3.81, 95% CI 1.10–13.2; Evidence level 2+). Failure to stop prolonged or excessive traction despite poor progress accounts for much malpractice litigation. Failed procedures, birth trauma, admission of a term baby to neonatal care, Apgar less than 7 at 5 minutes, or cord arterial pH less than 7.10 should prompt incident reporting and review where needed (Evidence level 4). More than three pulls and application greater than 12 minutes are linked to failed forceps and serious neonatal trauma; neonatal staff should monitor for injuries that may not be apparent immediately (Evidence level 2+). Disimpacting the head before caesarean after abandoned forceps is good practice; comparative effectiveness of manoeuvres and devices needs research.

document_sections.heading: 5.7. What is the role of episiotomy in preventing maternal pelvic floor morbidity at assisted vaginal birth?
document_sections.content: Discuss mediolateral episiotomy before assisted birth (P). Robust evidence does not establish either routine or restrictive use: individualise the decision to clinical circumstances and the woman’s preferences. Evidence for prevention of OASI is stronger in nulliparous women and with forceps (B). If performed, start the incision as the head distends the perineum and cut at a 60 degree angle (B). A two-centre RCT of 200 nulliparous women could not establish whether routine or restrictive episiotomy was preferable: OASI occurred in 8.1% of 99 women assigned routine use versus 10.9% of 101 assigned restrictive use (OR 0.72, 95% CI 0.28–1.87; Evidence level 1+). A Dutch observational study of 28 732 assisted births associated mediolateral episiotomy with lower OASI after vacuum (9.4% versus 1.4%; OR 0.11, 95% CI 0.09–0.13) and forceps (22.7% versus 2.6%; OR 0.28, 95% CI 0.13– 0.63); another Dutch cohort of 2861 births reported 5.7% OASI and a six-fold reduction with episiotomy. Conversely, a UK prospective series of 1360 births found no apparent OASI protection with vacuum (4.3% with versus 5.5% without episiotomy) or forceps (11.7% versus 10.6%), and more postpartum haemorrhage with episiotomy (28.4% versus 18.4%; OR 1.72, 95% CI 1.21–2.45). A UK retrospective analysis of 1.2 million primiparous vaginal births estimated OASIS risk without episiotomy as 1.89 (95% CI 1.74-2.05) times greater with ventouse and 6.53 times greater with forceps (95% CI 5.57-7.64; Evidence level 1+ to 2–). Two reviews, each including 15 observational vacuum-birth studies, disagreed: one considered mediolateral or lateral episiotomy protective in nulliparous women and advised considering it; the other found no apparent benefit in vacuum birth and possible increased maternal morbidity in parous women. For nulliparous women, the reviewed relationship with OASIS was not significant (OR 0.68, 95% CI 0.43–1.07; six studies); for parous women, risk increased (OR 1.27, 95% CI 1.05–1.53; two reports; Evidence level 1+).

document_sections.heading: 6.1. Should prophylactic antibiotics be given?
document_sections.content: Recommend one prophylactic intravenous dose of amoxicillin and clavulanic acid after assisted vaginal birth because it significantly lowers confirmed or suspected maternal infection versus placebo (A). Maintain good hygiene and aseptic practice (P). An earlier Cochrane review identified only one randomised trial of 393 participants: endometritis occurred in seven women without antibiotics and none given prophylaxis (RR 0.07, 95% CI 0.00–1.21). Evidence was similarly sparse for antibiotics after uncomplicated birth or episiotomy repair; stewardship remains important to limit resistance (Evidence level 1++). The blinded multicentre ANODE trial enrolled women after forceps or vacuum birth at 36 weeks or greater gestation across 27 UK hospital obstetric units; participants had no need for continuing postpartum antibiotics and no contraindication to the study antibiotic. Allocation to one intravenous dose or placebo was 1:1. Primary outcome events occurred in 486 [15%] of 3225 women. Confirmed or suspected infection affected 180 [11%] of 1619 women allocated amoxicillin and clavulanic acid versus 306 [19%] of 1606 allocated placebo (RR 0 58, 95% CI 0 49–0 69; P < 0 0001). Antibiotics were given a median of 3 hours after birth; recipients also had significantly less perineal wound infection, pain and wound breakdown, and fewer related primary-care, home and outpatient visits. The trial observed few intervention-related adverse events. Obstetricians should use aseptic technique and protective equipment such as gloves, aprons or gowns (Evidence level 4).

document_sections.heading: 6.2. Should thromboprophylaxis be given?
document_sections.content: Reassess venous-thromboembolism risk and the need for thromboprophylaxis following assisted birth (D). Evidence does not adequately isolate the procedure’s independent thromboembolism risk, although prolonged labour and immobility are shared risk factors for thromboembolism and operative birth. Prescribe prophylaxis according to reassessed risk and consult RCOG Green-top Guideline No. 37a (Evidence level 4).

document_sections.heading: 6.3. What analgesia should be given after birth?
document_sections.content: Unless contraindicated, routinely offer regular NSAIDs and paracetamol (A). Oral NSAIDs such as diclofenac or ibuprofen relieve perineal pain and provide better analgesia than paracetamol or placebo; paracetamol has an established postnatal safety record and is regularly used for postoperative pain (Evidence level 1++).

document_sections.heading: 6.4. What precautions should be taken for care of the bladder after birth?
document_sections.content: Explain postpartum urinary-retention risk and the importance of emptying the bladder (P). Monitor and document the time and volume of the first void (C), and measure post-void residual urine if retention is suspected (P). For a theatre trial with regional analgesia, recommend an indwelling catheter after birth to prevent unrecognised retention and remove it according to local protocol (P). Offer physiotherapy-directed approaches to lower urinary incontinence at 3 months (B). Assisted birth, prolonged labour and epidural analgesia are associated with postpartum urinary retention, potentially leading to long-term bladder dysfunction. Despite variation in UK practice, measure at least the first void and assess residual urine when indicated (Evidence level 2+). Trained staff may use bladder scanning instead of catheterisation to measure residual volume while avoiding confusion between the uterus and bladder (Evidence level 2++). A small before-and-after study suggested that intermittent catheterisation at 2 hours lowered unrecognised retention from 15/23 (65%) without that approach to 2/11 (18%) with it (P = 0.02), but its size and design introduce bias (Evidence level 2–). After regional analgesia for a theatre trial, offer an indwelling catheter for 6–12 hours under local policy, then use fluid-balance records to confirm adequate voiding (P). Better prevention and management studies are needed. Incontinence is common late in pregnancy and postpartum; a review found uncertain benefit from postnatal pelvic-floor muscle exercise as treatment. In one prevention trial involving women with assisted birth and/or a baby over 4 kg, physiotherapist-led intervention reduced incontinence at 3 months from 38.4% to 31.0%; the effect diminished at 12 months (Evidence level 1+).

document_sections.heading: 6.5. How can psychological morbidity be reduced for the woman?
document_sections.content: Shared decisions, effective communication and positive continuous support during labour and birth may lessen later psychological morbidity (P). Before discharge, review why assisted birth was undertaken, complication management and implications for future births; ideally the operating obstetrician conducts this discussion (P). Offer support to women wishing to discuss a traumatic birth and consider effects on their birth partner (P). Do not offer one high-intensity psychological session explicitly focused on reliving the trauma (P). At 1 month, refer women with persistent PTSD symptoms to appropriately skilled professionals according to NICE guidance (D). Psychological wellbeing has complex determinants. A Norwegian prospective cohort did not find delivery mode significantly associated with a change in emotional distress between 30 weeks of gestation and 6 months postpartum or with distress at 6 months; antenatal distress was its strongest postnatal predictor (Evidence level 2+). In a 2010 UK maternity survey, women after forceps versus unassisted birth more often reported two or more PTSD-type symptoms at 3 months (25/359 [7%] versus 93/3275 [3%]; OR 4.89, 95% CI 2.68–8.9). Among assisted-birth respondents, 42% had not discussed their birth with a professional; 43% of these wished to do so (Evidence level 2+). At 3 years after operative birth, a cohort reported that 50% did not plan another child, with almost one-half of that group citing fear of childbirth as the principal reason (Evidence level 2+). Studies of assisted birth and PTSD conflict; a review described assisted birth as one among several risk factors and proposed considering predisposition, triggers and coping (Evidence level 2+). Another cohort linked traumatic birth particularly to lack of control and lack of choice over pain relief, supporting attention to decision making, analgesia and non-technical skills (Evidence level 2+). A Cochrane review found little or no evidence that psychological debriefing either prevents or causes psychological trauma, although women report wanting a post-birth review about complications and future births (Evidence level 2–). Optimal review timing, setting and clinician remain uncertain; refer persistent severe symptoms to relevant expertise under NICE postnatal mental-health and PTSD guidance (Evidence level 4).

document_sections.heading: 6.6. What information should women be given for future births?
document_sections.content: Explain that spontaneous vaginal birth is highly likely in later labours after assisted vaginal birth (B). Individualise future care following a third- or fourth-degree perineal tear or persistent pelvic-floor morbidity (P). Encourage women after uncomplicated assisted birth to aim for spontaneous vaginal birth subsequently. A Swedish registry found that 90% of women with a first-birth ventouse procedure had a spontaneous or unassisted second birth. Repeat operative-birth risk exceeds that after an unassisted first birth, but its absolute level remains low. After more complex theatre-assisted births, approximately 80% achieved later spontaneous vaginal birth; discuss this early because decisions about future birth may form soon after delivery (Evidence level 2+). Review plans carefully after severe tears, particularly with symptoms, because subsequent birth may further damage the anorectum; counsel about recurrence and future delivery in accordance with the cited RCOG guidance (Evidence level 2+).

document_sections.heading: 7.1. What type of documentation should be completed for assisted vaginal birth?
document_sections.content: Record detailed assessment, decision making, procedure, postnatal plan and information needed for counselling about later pregnancies; use a standardised proforma (P). Record and process paired cord-blood samples after every attempted assisted vaginal birth (P). Failed birth, major obstetric haemorrhage, OASI, shoulder dystocia or substantial neonatal complications should prompt an incident report within risk-management processes (P). The procedural record should also capture critical times and support ongoing care, post-birth discussion and audit; Appendix 2 provides an example form.

document_sections.heading: 7.2. How should serious adverse events be dealt with?
document_sections.content: Keep ongoing care of the woman, baby and family foremost (P). Obstetricians must fulfil their duty of candour by being honest when care goes wrong (P). They should contribute to incident reports and confidential enquiries, undertake regular reviews and audits, address identified problems constructively, and retrain when necessary (P). Maternity units should support women, families and staff after serious events and foster a safe learning environment (P). Such events involve complex human factors and do not invariably arise from failures in care.

document_sections.heading: 8. Recommendations for future research
document_sections.content: Research priorities are second-stage oxytocin in women receiving epidural analgesia, early manual correction of fetal malposition, ultrasound assessment of head position before assisted birth, selection of an instrument for rotational birth, and manoeuvres for fetal-head impaction during second-stage caesarean birth. These are unresolved questions, not recommendations to use the interventions.

document_sections.heading: 9. Auditable topics
document_sections.content: Suggested unit audit includes the proportion of assisted vaginal births, against a UK average between 10% and 15%. Unit- and operator-level measures include unsuccessful attempts, sequential-instrument use, and review of care after failure or sequential use, including decisions to change or stop instruments and ultrasound confirmation of fetal position. Further measures are third- and fourth-degree tears, with cited rates of 1–4% for vacuum and 8–12% for forceps; composite neonatal trauma including subgaleal haemorrhage, brachial-plexus injury, fracture, facial-nerve palsy or cerebral haemorrhage; Apgar less than 7 at 5 minutes; and cord arterial pH less than 7.10. Audit documentation of verbal or written consent (100%), written consent for theatre trials (100%), complete records (100%), and postnatal review explaining the birth and future options (100%).

document_sections.heading: Appendix 1 Explanation of guidelines and evidence levels
document_sections.content: RCOG guidelines are systematically developed aids to decisions rather than exclusive treatment instructions; apply them in light of individual needs, institutional resources and local populations. Evidence levels are 1++ for high-quality randomised evidence with very low bias risk; 1+ for well-conducted randomised evidence with low bias risk; 1 for randomised evidence with high bias risk; 2++ for high-quality case–control or cohort evidence with very low confounding, bias or chance and high causal probability; 2+ for well-conducted observational evidence with low such risk and moderate causal probability; 2 for observational evidence with high such risk and substantial possibility of a noncausal relationship; 3 for non-analytical studies; and 4 for expert opinion. Recommendation grade A requires directly applicable, consistent high-level randomised evidence; B derives from directly applicable consistent 2++ evidence or extrapolation from 1++ or 1+; C derives from directly applicable consistent 2+ evidence or extrapolation from 2++; D derives from level 3 or 4 evidence or extrapolation from 2+. P denotes a good practice point based on the guideline development group’s clinical experience.

document_sections.heading: Appendix 2 Assisted vaginal birth record (revised)
document_sections.content: The appendix identifies a revised record for documenting assisted vaginal birth; the guideline refers to it as an example of standardised procedural documentation.

document_sections.heading: Appendix 3 Decision making for assisted vaginal birth
document_sections.content: The decision pathway begins by confirming safety criteria, choosing the birth setting and instrument, applying the instrument correctly, and rotating if indicated before traction. Consider a theatre trial if one-fifth of the head is abdominally palpable, the head is midpelvic, rotation is required or cephalopelvic disproportion is suspected. Continue in the labour room for a low-pelvic or outlet head, absent or easy rotation, and no such suspicion. Choose an instrument the operator or supervisor uses competently and that is least likely to fail, avoiding sequential use. Avoid vacuum at < 32 weeks gestation and exercise caution at 32–36 weeks. If correct application fails, reassess engagement, position, station and asynclitism; an inexperienced operator seeks a second opinion, while an experienced operator reassesses possible reapplication, instrument change or discontinuation. Stop if correct placement remains impossible. If gentle rotation fails, obtain senior review of placement and technique and stop if rotation remains unsuccessful; birth in direct OP position may occur with vacuum or low-station forceps. If traction produces no progressive descent, check placement and disproportion, obtain another opinion when inexperienced, and allow an experienced operator to revise the instrument or traction direction; stop if descent remains absent, and stop vacuum after two ‘pop offs’. Reassess after 3 pulls. Consider stopping vacuum if the head has not reached the pelvic floor, allowing a maximum of 3 gentle further pulls to pass the perineum, or forceps if crowning and imminent birth have not occurred. After failure, consider forceps following failed vacuum only when the vertex is low; weigh increased fetal trauma and OASI from sequential instruments against increased maternal morbidity from second-stage caesarean and fetal-head impaction risk. Inform the neonatologist of increased neonatal morbidity risk, complete the assisted-birth form and discuss the experience with the mother, partner and family.
